claims.text: The alloy contains equimolar W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr is a single-phase solid solution.
The initial WTaTiVZr alloy has high lattice distortion.
The initial WTaTiVZr alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Lattice strain from the multiple principal elements alters dislocation mobility in WTaTiVZr.
Under high-temperature loading, lattice distortion promotes nucleation of a high density of nanoscale deformation twins in WTaTiVZr.
Under high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr develops a complex, entangled dislocation network.
Deformation nanotwinning can facilitate plastic deformation and high ductility.
Nanoscale twins and dislocation structures impede crack propagation.
The combined nanotwinning and dislocation-network mechanism permits sustained plastic flow while resisting crack growth.
WTaTiVZr has significantly greater high-temperature toughness and ductility than pure tungsten because of the proposed nanoscale deformation mechanisms.
WTaTiVZr will have a lower ductile-brittle transition temperature than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will show higher plastic strain than pure tungsten under sustained high-temperature loading.
WTaTiVZr will show greater work hardening than pure tungsten under sustained high-temperature loading.
Commercially used pure tungsten has limited high-temperature plastic deformation and lower toughness because it lacks the proposed nanoscale deformation mechanisms.
The proposed mechanism remains operative up to approximately 1000 degrees Celsius if significant phase separation or precipitation does not occur.
Elevated-temperature creep behavior of TaTiVWZr has previously been investigated and compared with pure tungsten.
Identical tensile or creep tests at approximately 800 degrees Celsius, coupled with microscopy and diffraction, can compare the HEA with pure tungsten.
Failure to observe either improved mechanical outcomes or increased nanotwin and dislocation-network densities in the HEA would falsify the stated hypothesis.
